outcomes: A request that writes several rows commits them together or not at all, without the handler naming a transaction
A read-only request pays nothing for transactional mode: no reserved connection, no BEGIN
A cancelled request stops its database work rather than finishing it on a connection nobody is waiting for
A wedged handler cannot pin a pooled connection for ever
An operator can tell why a transaction rolled back without any log line carrying an error message, a bound parameter, or row data
nonGoals: Two-phase commit or any cross-datasource atomicity guarantee
Deriving the schema from the database: the table declarations in code are the source of truth
Hiding SQL — the query builder narrows what is easy to express, it does not replace the driver
Promising that a pre-1.0 minor release keeps the previous persistence contract

requirements.text: Entering transactional mode reserves no connection and issues no BEGIN. A connection is reserved and BEGIN is issued on the first write to a datasource, once per datasource, and concurrent writers await the same opening rather than opening twice.

The request-scoped unit of work finalizes at most once: a second commit or rollback is a no-op, a nested `runInTransaction` joins the outer unit instead of committing it, and finalizing after the ambient state was already resolved is a no-op rather than an error.

A unit spanning several datasources is best-effort, never two-phase: every reserved connection is released, and any COMMIT failure is surfaced as an error — as an AggregateError when more than one datasource failed — so a partial commit is never reported as success.

A transaction that exceeds its timeout is rolled back exactly once. A commit racing that timeout awaits the in-flight rollback and then fails, instead of committing connections the timeout already released.
A query started after the request signal aborted raises `QueryAbortError`, and a query already in flight is cancelled at the PostgreSQL protocol level rather than left running.

The transaction boundary record and the `sql.tx.rollback.<cause>` counter carry a classified cause code only. No error message, bound parameter value, or row datum is read or emitted, and a rollback record never carries an error object.
The transaction and concurrency behaviour is asserted against the shared cross-language corpus, so the TypeScript and Go adapters cannot drift on outcomes, causes, or metric names.

A project that declares tables emits the database and schemas it needs into its own infra requirements sidecar, including tables that live only in a dependency package, so deployment requirements are derived from code rather than restated by hand.
